assetSources.prompt:
Use case: historical-scene. Asset type: production sprite atlas for a 1835 Texas Revolution top-down town simulation. The two input images are style, palette, scale, outline, lighting and elevated-camera references only; create new historically distinct buildings. Produce one square 1254x1254 PNG, exactly 4 columns x 4 rows, sixteen isolated south-facing building sprites in strict reading order. TRUE transparent RGBA background; no checkerboard, scenery, terrain islands, labels, people, flags, signs, props outside buildings, borders, cell lines, or painted transparency. Keep every complete sprite wholly within its equal cell with at least 18px transparent gutter, ground-contact shadow contained inside the cell, consistent baseline and miniature world scale. Warm hand-illustrated frontier-v1 style: dark earthy brown outlines, restrained ochre wood and mud, weathered materials, clear readable silhouettes, slight elevated front-right view and upper-left light, not photoreal and not fantasy.
Row 1: (1) small one-storey sawn-timber frame building, pale weathered clapboard siding, shingle gable roof, glazed sash window and plank door; (2) storey-and-a-half frame store, taller clapboard walls, attic window in gable, shingle roof, sash windows, plank door; (3) two-storey four-room frame house resembling an early plain Texas civic residence, symmetrical clapboard front, two windows below and two above, centered door, simple shingle roof; (4) Whiteside Hotel of San Felipe: broad storey-and-a-half LOG dog-run house with two rooms flanking a clearly open central passage under one long roof, stick-and-mud chimney at each outer end, rough clapboards/shingles, no porch railing.
Row 2: (1) Round Top House of Victoria: round fortified two-level log or timber structure, heavy vertical-plank door, first-level gun slits, squat defensible silhouette, conical or polygonal shingled roof; (2) same Round Top House alternate weathered angle/condition, still round and fortified with gun slits and heavy door; (3) small upright-post jacal, sticks visible through pale mud daub, thatch gable roof, little door and tiny window; (4) broader jacal variant, uneven upright-post mud walls and thicker thatch roof.
Row 3: (1) narrow poorer jacal, patchy mud daub exposing woven sticks, low thatch roof; (2) jacal with a distinct open brush ramada attached at the front/side, ramada supported by thin posts, hut itself intact; (3) Mina frontier stockade: freestanding compact square enclosure of sharpened vertical logs with a visible gated front and a small log cabin enclosed within, read as one complete compound from the elevated view; (4) same Mina stockade alternate with gate open and enclosed cabin visible, compact complete compound.
Row 4: (1) Liberty Casa Consistorial, a small plain 22-foot-square hewn-log court room, centered plank door, two modest windows, shingle gable roof, civic but unornamented; (2) same Liberty court room alternate side-facing door/window arrangement; (3) simple clapboard commercial building variant with broad double plank shop door and two glazed sash windows; (4) modest one-storey frame residence variant with clapboards, one plank door, two sash windows and a small rear chimney.
Historical constraints: early 1830s Texas frontier construction; no Victorian trim, balconies, modern glass storefronts, brick rowhouse styling, stone castle towers, fantasy palisades, cannons, smoke, vegetation, roads, or background. Round Top House must read round and fortified, not as a normal square storehouse. Whiteside must visibly retain the open dog-run passage and two end chimneys. Stockade must be a complete enclosure, not loose fence segments. Output actual transparent alpha.
assetSources.postProcessing: None. Original built-in imagegen PNG copied byte-for-byte; read-only alpha and atlas-bound validation only.
assetSources.review: Sixteen clean south-facing structures. Distinct frames, Whiteside dog-run, two Round Top variants, four jacales, two Mina stockades, two Liberty court-room views, and two additional frame-building variants.

applicationIcon.origin: Supplied by the owner, 2026-09-11. Generated with ChatGPT and handed over as a PNG with a transparent field.
applicationIcon.postProcessing: Trimmed to the emblem, squared with transparent padding, and written as a multi-resolution .ico at 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 128 and 256 pixels. No recolouring and no redrawing.
applicationIcon.whereItAppears: The executable, and from there Explorer, the taskbar, the Start menu entry and the desktop shortcut, plus the title bar of every window the launcher opens.
applicationIcon.note: Decorative, and not a historical illustration. It is a general Texas emblem: the Alamo it shows is San Antonio in 1836, a different place and a later year than the Gonzales afternoon this prototype simulates. Nothing in the game reads it and it makes no historical claim.

launcherTitlePainting.origin: Supplied by the owner, 2026-09-20, after they drew a mockup of the launcher window and asked for it to be built. Handed over as a 1086 x 1448 opaque PNG with no lettering on it.
launcherTitlePainting.postProcessing: None. It is embedded in the launcher executable exactly as delivered and drawn scaled-to-cover, cropped at the sides and anchored 36% down so the sky, the flag and the chapel stay on the window. It is never stretched.
launcherTitlePainting.whereItAppears: Behind everything on the launcher window (launcher/TitleScene.cs). Nowhere else; the game itself does not read it.
launcherTitlePainting.whatItShows: The Alamo chapel at sunset under a heavy sky, a Lone Star flag on a rough timber pole, a field cannon on a spoked wheel at the right, a river in the middle distance, a column of silhouetted frontiersmen with long rifles at the lower left, and the left edge dissolving into cracked parchment carrying the outline of Texas and a star.
launcherTitlePainting.note: Decorative, and not a historical illustration, on the same terms as the emblem. The Alamo it shows is San Antonio, a different place and a later year than the Gonzales afternoon this prototype simulates; the masthead beneath it says Gonzales, 1835 because that is where the game is. Nothing in the simulation reads this picture and it makes no historical claim. The words COME AND TAKE IT in the window's top right corner are drawn by the launcher, not by the painting, and are part of the owner's mockup rather than a caption on the picture.

launcherButtonPlates.origin: Supplied by the owner, 2026-09-20, in three deliveries: seven plates first; then the stop sign, once it was pointed out that a green plate reading Start the class must never be the button that stops one; then the update badge, for the state rather than the action - the same button wearing a different face once a check has found a newer release. Each file name is the words cast into that plate.
launcherButtonPlates.postProcessing: None to the files. At start-up the launcher trims each one to the sign (the seven straight plates all sit within a pixel or two of x 136, y 161, 1902 x 348; the stop sign, a different picture at 1774 x 887, sits at x 30, y 96, 1715 x 674), resamples it once to 1600 pixels wide, and floods the black field away from the edge inwards so the chamfered corners and the stop sign's torn flag sit on the painting rather than in a black box. See launcher/PlateArt.cs.
launcherButtonPlates.whereItAppears: The buttons of the launcher window. The label and the mark are part of the picture, so the launcher writes nothing over a plate; the button's Text is still set, for the keyboard and the accessibility tree.
launcherButtonPlates.note: Decorative. The stop sign's torn Lone Star flag and its stop-hand roundel are design, not a depiction of an event.
launcherButtonPlates.alphaNote: button-update-available.png is the only one of the ten delivered with a real alpha channel (1536 x 1024, RGBA). It is cut to what its own alpha covers and composited as it is; it is never flooded or keyed, which would eat the darks in its red field. The other nine are opaque pictures on a black field and are flooded from the border inwards instead.

setupIcon.origin: Supplied by the owner, 2026-09-11, with the direction "this new image should be used for the installer. i like the one we are already using for the fully installed program." Generated with ChatGPT and handed over as a PNG with a transparent field.
setupIcon.postProcessing: Trimmed to the emblem, squared with transparent padding, and written as a multi-resolution .ico at 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 128 and 256 pixels. No recolouring and no redrawing. Same script and same treatment as the plain emblem.
setupIcon.whereItAppears: The executable itself, and therefore the downloaded setup file as Explorer and the browser show it. It does NOT appear on anything a teacher clicks after installing: the shortcuts, the window title bars and the Add/Remove listing are all pointed at the plain emblem instead.
setupIcon.whyTwo: One binary is both the setup program and the installed launcher, so it has one compiled icon resource. The download should look like a setup file and the installed program should not. The compiled resource is therefore the setup emblem and the plain emblem travels as an embedded resource, written beside the installed copy. The installed .exe seen in Explorer is the one place they diverge, because a single-file bundle cannot have its icon rewritten after publishing without breaking the bundle.
setupIcon.note: Decorative, and not a historical illustration, on the same terms as the plain emblem. The download arrow and carton are modern interface iconography and make no claim about 1835.
